content.text: {"primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, 'tartaroō' (the verb form of Tartarus, appearing only once in the New Testament) is understood to mean that God cast the angels who sinned into a place or condition of imprisonment and gloomy darkness where they are held in restraint awaiting final judgment. It is typically treated as a temporary intermediate prison for fallen angels — distinct from Gehenna (the final hell of punishment) and from Hades (the general realm of the dead) — with the word deliberately borrowed from Greek cosmology, where Tartarus was the deepest abyss below Hades reserved for the punishment of divine beings (e.g., the Titans). Peter's use is generally read as appropriating that familiar Hellenistic image to describe divine confinement of rebellious angels, not as an endorsement of Greek mythology.", "primary_basis": ["2 Peter 2:4 (the sole biblical occurrence: God 'cast them into Tartarus' and committed them to chains/pits of gloomy darkness, kept until judgment)", "Jude 6 (parallel passage: angels who did not keep their proper domain kept in eternal chains under darkness for the judgment of the great day)", "1 Peter 3:19-20 (the 'spirits in prison' associated with the days of Noah, often linked to the same imprisoned beings)", "Genesis 6:1-4 (the 'sons of God' episode, widely cited as the sin in view, especially via Second Temple tradition)", "1 Enoch 6-21 (extra-biblical but routinely cited as the interpretive background: the Watchers bound in a dark abyss until judgment)", "Luke 8:31 and Revelation 9:1-11; 20:1-3 (the 'abyss' as a comparable prison for demonic beings)"], "alternatives": [{"meaning": "Tartarus as simply 'hell' — identified or conflated with the final place of punishment (Gehenna). This reading is embedded in older English translations (KJV and others render tartaroō as 'cast down to hell') and persists in popular preaching that treats Tartarus, Hades, and Gehenna interchangeably.", "basis": ["2 Peter 2:4 as rendered 'hell' in the KJV and similar translations", "Matthew 25:41 (eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels, read as the same destiny)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Tartarus as the deepest compartment or lowest region of Hades/Sheol within a tiered cosmology of the underworld — a view found in some patristic and later systematic treatments that map Tartarus as a distinct sub-region of the intermediate state.", "basis": ["2 Peter 2:4", "Luke 16:19-31 (compartmentalized afterlife imagery)", "Greek cosmological background (Tartarus below Hades in Homer and Hesiod)"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "Tartarus as a debased condition rather than a location — the fallen angels were cast into a state of deepest spiritual darkness and abasement, cut off from God's light, not confined in a literal place. This is notably the Jehovah's Witnesses' interpretation but also appears in some other non-spatial readings.", "basis": ["2 Peter 2:4 read as describing condition, not geography", "Jude 6 (loss of original position/estate)"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "Tartarus as a purely literary or rhetorical borrowing from Greco-Roman mythology and Hellenistic Jewish literature, functioning as a vivid metaphor for certain divine judgment rather than teaching any specific cosmological doctrine. Common in critical scholarship, which stresses 2 Peter's dependence on 1 Enoch and Hellenistic idiom.", "basis": ["2 Peter 2:4 in light of 1 Enoch and Hellenistic Jewish usage (e.g., Josephus, Philo, Sibylline Oracles use Tartarus language)", "Jude 6 and its explicit debt to Enochic tradition (cf. Jude 14-15)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Divergence on the referent of the imprisoned angels: rather than the Genesis 6 Watchers, some (especially in older Reformed and dispensational teaching) read 'the angels who sinned' as those who fell with Satan in a primeval rebellion before Eden, making Tartarus the holding place from that original fall.", "basis": ["2 Peter 2:4", "Isaiah 14:12-15 and Ezekiel 28:12-17 (traditionally applied to Satan's fall)", "Revelation 12:4, 7-9"], "prominence": "common"}], "has_settled_consensus": true, "confidence": "high", "notes": "The term appears exactly once in the Bible (2 Peter 2:4, as the verb tartarōsas), so all interpretation rests on that single verse plus parallels. There is broad scholarly and much popular consensus on the core idea — a dark confinement of fallen angels pending judgment, using imagery borrowed from Greek and Enochic tradition — but genuine divergence persists on (a) whether Tartarus is a place or a condition, (b) whether it is distinct from or identical to 'hell'/Gehenna, and (c) which angelic fall is in view (Genesis 6 Watchers vs. Satan's primeval rebellion). Modern academic commentary strongly favors the Enochic/Genesis 6 background; older translations' rendering 'hell' has kept the conflated popular reading alive."}
